clinicalPearls: The most common congenital heart malformation, an opening in the interventricular septum that permits shunting between the ventricles; most are membranous or muscular in location.

The direction and size of the shunt depend on the defect size and the relative resistances of the pulmonary and systemic circulations, so many defects become clinically apparent only as pulmonary resistance falls in the first weeks of life.
Small defects produce a loud, often harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border but little haemodynamic burden, and many close spontaneously.
Large defects cause a significant left-to-right shunt with excessive pulmonary blood flow, leading to heart failure signs such as tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, and failure to thrive in infancy.
A large shunt may generate a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex from increased flow across the mitral valve.
Untreated large defects risk progressive pulmonary vascular disease that can eventually reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger physiology), a late and largely irreversible complication.
Echocardiography defines the defect location and size, estimates shunt magnitude, and assesses chamber enlargement and pulmonary pressures.

Management of a haemodynamically significant defect focuses on treating heart failure and supporting growth, with surgical or catheter closure for defects that do not shrink or that cause failure or pulmonary hypertension.
Many small muscular and membranous defects close on their own during early childhood.
reference.pathophysiology: A communication in the ventricular septum allows blood to shunt according to the pressure and resistance gradient between the ventricles. After birth, as pulmonary vascular resistance declines, left-to-right shunting increases, raising pulmonary blood flow and volume-loading the left atrium and left ventricle. A large, sustained shunt increases pulmonary artery pressure and flow, and over time medial hypertrophy and intimal changes in the pulmonary vasculature raise resistance irreversibly; when pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic, the shunt reverses and produces cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome).
additionalDifferentials: Tetralogy of Fallot with a dominant VSD murmur
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to localise the defect and quantify shunt and chamber size
Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora in large shunts
Electrocardiogram for left or biventricular hypertrophy
Assessment of growth and feeding as markers of shunt significance
Cardiac catheterisation to measure pulmonary vascular resistance when pulmonary hypertension is suspected
redFlags: Signs of congestive heart failure in infancy: tachypnoea, feeding difficulty, sweating, and failure to thrive
Development of pulmonary hypertension or a shrinking left-to-right shunt suggesting rising pulmonary resistance
New cyanosis or a diminishing murmur indicating shunt reversal (Eisenmenger physiology)
Poor weight gain despite medical therapy
Signs of infective endocarditis in a child with a known defect
reference.prognosis: Small defects have an excellent outlook and often close spontaneously. Large defects, if repaired before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops, generally have a good outcome; delayed closure risks fixed pulmonary hypertension and a markedly worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Assuming a loud murmur means a large, dangerous defect when small defects are often the loudest
Missing a large defect in the newborn period before pulmonary resistance falls and the murmur becomes apparent
Overlooking progression to pulmonary vascular disease by delaying closure of a significant shunt
Attributing poor growth to feeding problems rather than an underlying significant shunt
Failing to recognise shunt reversal when cyanosis appears in a previously acyanotic child
management: Manage small defects expectantly with observation, as many close spontaneously, alongside dental hygiene and endocarditis awareness
Treat the heart failure of a large left-to-right shunt medically with diuretics and afterload reduction using ACE inhibitors, plus high-calorie nutritional support for faltering growth
Close large or symptomatic defects surgically with a patch, or by transcatheter device closure in suitable cases, before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops
Monitor with serial echocardiography for shunt size, chamber loading and rising pulmonary pressures
Once Eisenmenger physiology is established, avoid defect closure and manage with pulmonary vasodilator therapy, counselling against pregnancy
Provide ongoing multidisciplinary paediatric and congenital cardiology follow-up
